info.title: ResolveAI API
info.summary: AI-powered helpdesk and incident triage platform
info.description:
ResolveAI triages support tickets, tracks business-hours SLAs, correlates ticket
storms into incidents, and drafts grounded replies from a tenant knowledge base.

**The governing principle of the whole API: AI produces signals, deterministic code
makes decisions.** The model never returns a priority — it returns observations
(`category`, `reportedImpact`, `paymentAffected`, `linguisticUrgency`), and a versioned
rule set turns those into a priority. `GET /tickets/{id}/priority-rationale` exposes both
halves separately so a wrong answer can be attributed to the model or to the policy.

### Conventions that apply everywhere

- Every path is prefixed `/api/v1`. The API is versioned as a whole, never per endpoint.
- All errors are RFC 7807 `application/problem+json`. Clients switch on `errorCode`,
  never on `detail`, which is human prose and may change.
- All timestamps are ISO 8601, UTC, `Z`-suffixed. Never epoch millis.
- JSON is `camelCase`; enum values are `SCREAMING_SNAKE` strings.
- List responses are wrapped in `{ data, pagination }`, never a bare array.
- Cursor pagination on live queues, offset pagination on slow-moving admin lists.
  Offset on a live queue is not merely slow, it is **wrong**: a ticket resolved on page 1
  shifts the set and page 2 silently skips a row the agent never saw.
- Cross-tenant and cross-customer reads return **404, not 403**. A 403 confirms the
  resource exists and turns every id into a probe.
- Tokens are never accepted as query parameters — access logs, browser history and
  `Referer` headers all leak them. `Authorization` header only.

post.description:
Registers a customer under an existing tenant, identified by slug. Agents, leads and
admins are created by an admin and never self-register.

**The `409` does leak whether an email is registered with a tenant.** Accepted
deliberately: a portal that silently swallows a duplicate registration produces a
worse failure — the user cannot log in and does not know why. Mitigated by a 5/hour
per-IP rate limit.

post.summary: Exchange credentials for an access token and a rotating refresh token
post.description:
**A single `401 INVALID_CREDENTIALS` covers all three failure causes** — no such
user, wrong password, wrong tenant. Distinguishing them turns login into a
user-enumeration oracle. Response time is padded to a constant by always running a
BCrypt comparison, against a dummy hash when the user does not exist, so timing does
not leak what the status code does not.

401.description: `INVALID_CREDENTIALS` — wrong email, wrong password, or no such user.

403.description: `ACCOUNT_DISABLED` — account or tenant deactivated.

post.summary: Rotate the access token; consumes the presented refresh token
post.description:
Returns a new access token **and a new refresh token**. The presented token is
consumed.

**Reuse detection:** presenting a token whose `used_at` is already set means either
the token was stolen and replayed, or the legitimate client is replaying. The system
cannot tell which party is the attacker, so it **revokes the entire `family_id`** and
forces a fresh login. That is the standard refresh-token-rotation defence.

401.description:
`INVALID_REFRESH_TOKEN` — unknown, expired or revoked.
`TOKEN_REUSE_DETECTED` — already used; the whole token family is now revoked.

post.summary: Create a ticket; triage runs asynchronously
post.description:
Commits the ticket **and an outbox event in one transaction** and returns
immediately. That single transaction is what removes the dual-write problem: there is
no window in which a ticket exists but its triage job does not, and no window in
which a job exists for a ticket that was rolled back.

**`202`, not `201`, and this is the interview question.** The resource *is* created,
which normally argues for `201`. But the response deliberately advertises
`analysisStatus: "PROCESSING"`, and `priority`, `category`, `assignee` and `team` are
all still null and **will change without any further client action**. `202` tells the
client to poll the status resource; `201` would imply the representation is final.

> **This endpoint returned `201` in Phase 5 and returns `202` from Phase 6.** In
> Phase 5 there was no outbox and no async triage, so the representation *was*
> final and `202` would have been a lie. The change landed in its own commit, which
> is the point: the status code follows the semantics rather than being chosen once
> and defended afterwards.

**`body` is capped at 20,000 characters as a security control**, not a tidiness rule.
Every ticket triggers an LLM call, so an uncapped body is a token-cost denial of
service.

**Idempotency:** replaying the same key with the same body returns the original `202`
verbatim, including the same `id`. The same key with a *different* body is `422`,
never a silent replay of the wrong response.

get.description:
**What the caller can see is determined by role, not by a query parameter**, and the
scoping is applied server-side and is not overridable:

| Role | Sees |
|---|---|
| `CUSTOMER` | only tickets where `requester_id = me` |
| `AGENT` | tickets assigned to them **or** in their team's queue |
| `TEAM_LEAD` | all tickets in their team |
| `ADMIN` | all tickets in the tenant |

**Cursor pagination, not `page`/`offset`, and the reason is correctness rather than
speed.** Tickets resolve out of a filtered set while an agent is paging through it.
With `OFFSET`, resolving a ticket on page 1 shifts everything up by one and **page 2
silently skips a ticket the agent never saw.** The cursor encodes `(created_at, id)`
and is stable under concurrent mutation.

There is no `totalElements`: counting a filtered set on every page is expensive and
nobody uses the number.

get.description:
**Field visibility by role is enforced in the response mapper by returning a
different DTO, not by null-setting fields on a shared one.** A `CUSTOMER` never
receives `INTERNAL` messages, `priorityRationale`, `analysisStatus`, `latestDraftId`
or the internal SLA detail. A shared DTO with `if (role != CUSTOMER) ...` is one
forgotten branch away from leaking internal notes; separate types make the leak a
compile error.

**`404`, never `403`, for a ticket in another tenant or belonging to another
customer.** A `403` would confirm the ticket exists, which is an information leak.
`403` is reserved for "you are authenticated, this resource is in your scope, but this
*action* is not permitted".

The `ETag` response header carries the entity `version` and is required back as
`If-Match` on every mutation.

post.summary: Add a public reply or an internal note
post.description:
**An agent's first `PUBLIC` message stops the first-response SLA clock in the same
transaction**, and `slaEffect` in the response is the important field. One transaction
is what closes the race against the SLA poller: an agent replying at the exact instant
a breach would fire cannot produce both a first response and a breach. Returning the
effect means the UI does not have to re-fetch to discover it.

post.description:
**This is the endpoint with the concurrency test behind it.** The claim is a
conditional update with an affected-row check, not a `SELECT` followed by an `UPDATE`:

```sql
UPDATE ticket
   SET assignee_id = :agentId, status = 'ASSIGNED', version = version + 1
 WHERE id = :ticketId AND assignee_id IS NULL;
-- affected rows = 0 → someone else won → 409 ALREADY_ASSIGNED
```

Two agents clicking "Assign to me" in the same millisecond produce exactly one `200`
and one `409`. An integration test drives 20 concurrent requests and asserts exactly
that distribution.

post.description:
**Illegal transitions are rejected by the server, not prevented by the UI.** The
permitted graph:

```
OPEN                → TRIAGED, ASSIGNED, CLOSED
TRIAGED             → ASSIGNED, CLOSED
ASSIGNED            → IN_PROGRESS, WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER, PENDING_THIRD_PARTY, RESOLVED, OPEN
IN_PROGRESS         → WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER, PENDING_THIRD_PARTY, RESOLVED, ASSIGNED
WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER → IN_PROGRESS, RESOLVED, CLOSED          ← SLA clock PAUSES on entry
PENDING_THIRD_PARTY → IN_PROGRESS, RESOLVED                  ← SLA clock PAUSES on entry
RESOLVED            → CLOSED, OPEN
CLOSED              → terminal; reopening goes through /reopen
```

A rejection returns the **permitted targets** in `allowedTransitions`, so a client can
recover without hard-coding the state machine.

get.description:
**`200`, never `404` or `503`, for the `UNAVAILABLE` case.** The analysis resource
exists and its state is "we tried and failed". That is a successful read of a
legitimate state, and the ticket remains fully workable. Returning an error status
would make a degraded AI feature look like a broken API.

**Note what the model returns and what it does not.** There is no `priority` field
here. The model reports observations — category, impact, whether a payment is
involved, how urgent the language is — and a versioned rule set turns those into a
priority. See `GET /tickets/{id}/priority-rationale`.

**`extractedEntities.orderRef` reads `«ORDER_1»`.** The order reference was
PII-redacted before the text left for the model, so the model never saw the real
value and the placeholder is what comes back. Rehydration happens only when rendering
for an authorised human.

get.summary: Signals, policy evaluation and result — the endpoint that makes the AI auditable
get.description:
**Why this endpoint exists at all:** `inputs` separates `fromModel` from
`fromSystem`, and `rules` shows the deterministic evaluation, rule by rule, including
the ones that did *not* match.

When an agent overrides a priority, this structure makes it possible to tell whether
**the model misread the ticket** or **the policy is wrong** — two completely
different bugs with two completely different fixes. A design where the LLM simply
returns `"priority": "P2"` makes that distinction unrecoverable.

Every override is stored as a label, which is what makes the policy improvable rather
than merely arguable.

post.description:
**`402 Payment Required` is the honest code for an exhausted AI budget.** It is
rarely used, semantically exact, and distinguishable from `429` — which matters,
because a client should retry after a `429` and must **not** after a `402`.

get.summary: The draft, with a verdict and citations for every claim
get.description:
**The most important response body in the API.** Three things to point at:

1. **Claim 3 is returned, not hidden.** It was dropped from `assembledText`
   (`kept: false`), but the agent can see that the model tried to invent a refund
   amount and a date, and *why* it was rejected. Hiding rejections would make the
   verification mechanism invisible and therefore untrustworthy. That rejection cost
   **zero LLM calls** — the numeric pre-filter caught it before the entailment
   verifier ran.
2. **`unresolvedAspects` is the most useful field for the agent.** A support agent's
   real question is not "what does the KB say" but *"what am I going to have to figure
   out myself?"*
3. **`tier: AUTHORITATIVE`** distinguishes a runbook from a resolved ticket. The agent
   should weigh *"the runbook says"* differently from *"someone did this once"*.

**When coverage falls below the threshold, `assembledText` is `null` — not a hedged
draft.** The design position is that a confidently wrong answer is worse than no
answer. The refusal suite in CI asserts this path fires 100% of the time on the
no-coverage fixtures.

**This is the quality-measurement endpoint, and it must be called even on discard.**
Without the discards the acceptance rate is measured only over the drafts that were

`editDistance` is computed server-side (Levenshtein, `assembledText` vs `finalText`)
and is **never trusted from the client**.

get.summary: Both clocks, with their full segment history
get.description:
**The `segments` array is the whole design, exposed.** `elapsedBusinessMinutes` is a
`SUM()` over `RUNNING` segments — there is no stored counter anywhere, so there is no
counter to drift, and pause/resume is an append, never an update.

`nextDeadlineAt` is `null` while paused, which is exactly why the poller
(`WHERE state = 'RUNNING' AND next_deadline_at <= NOW()`) skips it. The poller is
`O(due)`, not `O(open)`.

**`prediction.basis` names the statistic and the sample size**, so the number is
inspectable rather than magical. **This is not an LLM output** — it is a p75 window
function over 90 days of history. A percentile is faster, cheaper, more accurate and
explainable; using a model here would be worse on every axis.

prediction.basis: p75 over 90 days for (PAYMENT, P2, Payments team), n=214

post.description:
Closes the open `RUNNING` segment, inserts a new `PAUSED` segment, sets
`state='PAUSED'` and `next_deadline_at=NULL`, all in one transaction.

**Pausing an already-paused clock returns `200` with the existing state, not an
error.** The operation is naturally idempotent and the client should not have to check
first. The partial unique index `uq_segment_open` means two concurrent pause requests
cannot both insert an open segment; the loser gets a constraint violation which the
service maps to that same `200` replay, because the desired end state was reached
either way.

post.summary: Age a ticket's clocks — local profile only
post.description:
**A demo affordance, not part of the product surface.** The escalation ladder is
the most interesting behaviour in the SLA engine and the least demonstrable:
showing a rung fire honestly means waiting out half of a business-hours target.
This moves a ticket's clocks into the past so the next poll does what an hour of
waiting would have done.

**It rewrites the clock segments, not only the deadline.** The poller re-checks
elapsed against the rung under the row lock before firing — the guard that stops a
pause landing between claim and process from firing a rung the clock has not
reached — so shifting the deadline alone would be rescheduled rather than fired.

`@Profile("local")`: the bean does not exist under `prod` or `test`, the same guard
the seed loader uses. `ADMIN` in addition, and it logs at `WARN`, because an
endpoint that rewrites audit history should never be quiet about it.

parameters.name: minutes
parameters.description:
How far back to move them. 40 puts a P2 first-response clock (60-minute
target) past its 50% rung; 500 puts a resolution clock past all four.

example.note: The next poll (<=10s) will fire whatever rungs this crossed.

Ranked by `riskScore`, which compares the **predicted** resolution time against the
**remaining** budget. A ticket with 34 minutes left and a p75 of 180 is at risk even
though it has not breached anything yet — which is the point of predicting rather than
reporting.

`PROPOSED` incidents are what the correlation gate produced and no human has ruled on
yet. They are shown separately because **confirming one is a judgement call the
system deliberately does not make on its own**, and because every confirm or reject
writes a label into the evaluation set.

get.summary: Incident detail, linked tickets, updates and detection evidence
get.description:
**The `detection` object exposes the deterministic gate's evidence.**
`arrivalRateMultiple: 12.6` against `minRateMultiple: 3.0` is the record of *why* this
was proposed — and it makes clear that a statistical check, not a model, made that
call.

**`titleGeneratedBy` is a separate field precisely to show that the model's
contribution was the title and nothing else.** When it is `null`, the title was
templated because the LLM was unavailable — and the incident was still detected,
because detection never depended on the model.

`timeToDetectSeconds: 37` is a headline metric and it comes straight out of the
schema rather than a stopwatch.

`detachedTickets` keeps the soft-detached links visible — a ticket that fell out of
the storm is still part of the record — separately from the currently-live
`linkedTickets`.

post.summary: PROPOSED → CONFIRMED; also writes an evaluation label
post.description:
**`firstResponseClocksUnaffected` is a deliberate product decision, surfaced in the
response.** When a ticket joins an incident the *resolution* clock pauses — resolution
now depends on the incident, not the agent. The *first-response* clock keeps running,
because **the customer still deserves an acknowledgement even during an outage.**
There is no universally correct answer here; the response makes the choice visible
rather than hiding it.

Every confirm and every reject writes an `eval_case` row, which is how the correlation
gate acquires ground truth from ordinary use rather than from a labelling session.

A **soft** detach: `detached_at` is set, the row is kept. The link history is part of

of what the correlator actually did.

post.description:
Resumes every paused resolution clock. `resolveLinkedTickets` defaults to `true`,
which also moves every still-open linked ticket to `RESOLVED`; ticket resolution
failures do not fail the incident resolve — they come back in `skipped`.

post.summary: Publish an update; fans out to every linked ticket
post.description:
`202` because the fan-out is **queued**, not complete. The `links.deliveries` link is
the status resource.

**Fan-out is N independent, individually-retryable deliveries, not one broadcast.**
Delivery 23 failing means ticket 88322 retries and the other 37 customers are not
re-notified. `uq_delivery (incident_update_id, ticket_id)` guarantees that a
redelivered outbox event cannot double-message a customer.

`visibility` defaults to `INTERNAL` — a message is team-facing until someone
deliberately marks it `PUBLIC` for fan-out to customers.

`Idempotency-Key` is **required** here because this sends messages to real people.
`force: true` bypasses the `TOO_MANY_LINKED_TICKETS` guard on an incident linked to
more than 500 tickets, so an accidental fan-out to thousands of customers is not the
default.

so that **drafts already citing them can still resolve their citations** — a citation

post.description:
**`documentsSkipped` with its reason is deliberate.** Reindex cost is proportional to
*changed* documents, because `content_sha256` lets the indexer skip the rest.
`force: true` exists but reports its estimated cost up front, since a forced full
reindex on a large corpus is the single easiest way to burn the monthly AI budget by
accident.

get.summary: Hybrid lexical + vector retrieval, and the retrieval debugger
get.description:
**The score breakdown under `explain=true` is the point of this endpoint.** In the
example below, chunk 33401 ranked **1st lexically but only 3rd by vector**, and 33409
was the reverse. Neither retrieval method alone would have surfaced both at the top —
which is the argument for hybrid search, visible as data rather than asserted.

Fusion is **Reciprocal Rank Fusion**, which combines *ranks*, not scores, because
`ts_rank_cd` and cosine distance are on incomparable scales and normalising them
would be inventing a comparison that does not exist.

`kbVersion` is in the response because it is part of the retrieval cache key — any KB
edit makes previously cached results unreachable automatically, with no explicit
eviction.

parameters.description: Include the per-retriever rank and score breakdown.

post.summary: Reserve an attachment and get a presigned upload URL
post.description:
Step one of a two-step upload. Two security properties, both non-negotiable:

- **`storageKey` is a generated UUID, never the user's filename.** A filename-derived
  path invites traversal; a guessable one invites IDOR.
- **The declared `mimeType` is not trusted.** `/complete` re-reads the object and
  verifies the **actual magic bytes**; a `.exe` renamed `.png` is rejected there, not
  here.

`attachmentIds`** on a ticket or message.

about it prevents a support ticket about your support system.

get.description:
The gate every model call is checked against. Read before **every** call and
cached in Redis for five minutes, evicted on update — so switching external
models off takes effect immediately rather than within the TTL.

**A tenant with no policy row is treated as AI-disabled**, never as permissive
defaults. A missing row usually means a tenant provisioned by a path that forgot
to create one, and the two ways of guessing wrong are not symmetrical: guess
"disabled" and somebody files a bug that triage is not running; guess "allowed"
and a customer's messages have already gone to a third party they never agreed
to. This endpoint creates the row with restrictive defaults rather than 404ing,
so an admin always sees the five settings that govern them.

`currentMonthSpendMicros` is read-only here — it is moved by usage, never by an
admin, because an editable spend counter is a way to make the bill say anything.

put.description:
Setting `externalModelAllowed: false` with no local model configured makes every
draft request return `503 AI_DISABLED_BY_POLICY`. That is the correct outcome — the
policy is a hard gate, not a preference — and the response warns about it rather than
silently degrading.

**A full `PUT`, not a `PATCH`.** Five fields, read together before every model
call; a partial update of a safety setting is how one thing gets changed and
another silently kept. Sending the whole object means the admin has seen all five.

**No tenant id in the path**: it comes from the authenticated caller, so an admin
can only ever change their own tenant's policy. A `/admin/tenants/{id}/ai-policy`
shape would need an authorization check that this one cannot forget.

included) already records — no separate instrumentation. `suppressionRate` is set
on drafting rows only. `from` / `to` / `groupBy` from the original design are
**not implemented**: month to date is what the budget is measured against.

get.description:
**Reporting `claimLevelGroundedness` and `responseLevelGroundedness` side by side is
the point.** The gap between them *is* the finding: response-level averaging hides
unsupported claims inside otherwise-good answers, which is exactly the failure mode
where a metric reads 0.92 while a claim-level audit finds 30% hallucination.

The `REFUSAL` suite gate requires `refusalRate: 1.0` exactly. A confidently wrong
answer is worse than no answer, so 19 of 20 is a failure, not a 95%.

bearerAuth.description:
`Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>` from `POST /auth/login` or `/auth/refresh`.
Access tokens live 900 seconds.

**Tokens are never accepted as a query parameter.** They end up in access logs,
browser history and `Referer` headers, none of which are under this application's

TicketId.name: id
TicketId.description: Ticket id. Not the `TKT-…` reference, which is the tenant-facing label.

Cursor.name: cursor
Cursor.description:
Opaque cursor from the previous page's `pagination.nextCursor`. Base64 of
`{"c":"<created_at>","i":<id>}`. Omit for the first page.

Size.name: size
Size.description: Page size. Clamped server-side rather than rejected.

Page.name: page
Page.description: Zero-based page index. Offset pagination, used only on slow-moving admin lists.

IdempotencyKey.name: Idempotency-Key
IdempotencyKey.description:
Client-generated key, 16–128 characters of `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` — the character class is
constrained because the value becomes a Redis key.

Same key + same body replays the original response verbatim. Same key + different body
is `422`, never a silent replay of the wrong response.

IfMatch.name: If-Match
IfMatch.description:
The `ETag` from the last read of this resource. Required on every ticket and incident
mutation; a stale value is `409 VERSION_CONFLICT`.

ETag.description: Weak ETag carrying the entity `version`. Send it back as `If-Match`.

Unauthorized.description: `UNAUTHORIZED` — missing, malformed or expired access token.

Forbidden.description:
`FORBIDDEN` — authenticated, the resource is in your scope, but **this action** is not
permitted. Never used for a resource you cannot see; that is `404`.

TicketNotFound.description:
`TICKET_NOT_FOUND`. Also returned when the ticket belongs to another tenant, or to
another customer — **`404`, never `403`.** A `403` would confirm the ticket exists,
turning every id into a probe.

VersionConflict.description: `VERSION_CONFLICT` — the `If-Match` ETag is stale. Reload and retry.

example.title: Version conflict
example.detail: Ticket 88213 was modified by another user. Reload and retry.

PreconditionRequired.description: `PRECONDITION_REQUIRED` — `If-Match` was absent or unparseable on a mutation that requires it.

example.title: Precondition required
example.detail: This request must be conditional. Send the current ETag as If-Match.

ValidationError.description: `VALIDATION_ERROR` — one entry in `errors` per rejected field.

RateLimited.description: `RATE_LIMITED`. `Retry-After` says when. Retrying is correct here, unlike after a `402`.

AiPolicyView.description:
A tenant's AI settings. Everything here is read before a model call; nothing here
is advisory.

allowedProviders.description:
An allow-list. **Empty means "any configured provider"**, which is different
from "none" — that is what `externalModelAllowed: false` is for.

currentMonthSpendMicros.description: Moved by usage only. Micros, never a decimal — money in a double accumulates rounding error across a month of per-call increments.

budgetRemainingMicros.description:
Can go slightly negative. Two concurrent calls can both pass the pre-call
budget check and jointly overshoot by up to one call's cost — a deliberate,
bounded race, accepted because closing it means serialising every model call
behind a lock. The recorded *total* is exact regardless: spend is an atomic
SQL increment, not a read-modify-write.

props.description: At most 12 keys; values are numbers, booleans or strings of up to 80 characters.

ResponseTarget.description:
The customer's first-response promise — only the promise: no segments, escalation
rungs or breach prediction. `null` until triage has decided the priority.

allOf.description:
What a `CUSTOMER` receives for their own ticket: PUBLIC messages only, and the
first-response promise instead of the internal SLA detail.

Problem.description:
RFC 7807. **`errorCode` is the machine-readable contract** — clients switch on it,
never on `detail`, which is human prose and may change without a version bump.

**`traceId` is the OpenTelemetry trace id**, so a user reporting an error hands you a
string that finds the exact request across the async worker boundary.

detail.description: Human prose. Never parsed by a client.

code.description: The Bean Validation annotation that failed.

rejectedValue.description:
**Truncated and redacted.** Never echo a 27 KB body, or anything that
might contain PII, back into an error response or a log.

allowedTransitions.description: The permitted targets from the current state, so a client can recover without hard-coding the state machine.

CursorPage.description:
Cursor pagination, used on live queues. **No `totalElements`** — counting a filtered
set on every page is expensive and nobody uses the number.

nextCursor.description: Pass back as `cursor`. `null` on the last page.

OffsetPage.description:
Offset pagination, used only on small, slow-changing, admin-facing sets where a page
count is genuinely useful and drift is not a concern.

Priority.description: `UNTRIAGED` until the triage worker and the priority policy have run.

IncidentStatus.description: `MITIGATED` sits between `CONFIRMED` and `RESOLVED`: a manual annotation that the cause is understood and traffic is recovering, before every linked ticket is individually closed.

AnalysisStatus.description: `UNAVAILABLE` is a legitimate terminal state and is returned with `200`, not an error status.

ClaimVerdict.description:
`FAILED_NUMERIC_CHECK` is produced by the **numeric pre-filter**, before any
entailment call — it costs zero tokens and catches the most common and most damaging
hallucination, an invented amount or date.

email.description: Normalised to lowercase. Unique per tenant among non-deleted users.

refreshToken.description: Rotated on every use. The presented one is consumed.

permissions.description:
**For hiding buttons, never for enforcing anything.** The server remains the
only authority; this array exists so the frontend does not re-derive
authorization from the role string and drift out of sync with it.

body.description:
**The upper bound is a security control**, not tidiness. Every ticket triggers an
LLM call, so an uncapped body is a token-cost denial of service.

attachmentIds.description: Each must exist, be owned by the caller, be `/complete`d, and be unattached.

onBehalfOf.description: AGENT+ only. A CUSTOMER sending this gets `403`.

TicketCreatedResponse.description:
`priority`, `category`, `assignee` and `team` are null **and will change without any
further client action** — which is what `202` communicates and `201` would not.

SlaSummary.description: The compact form carried on list rows. The full segment history is on `GET /tickets/{id}/sla`.

TicketBase.description:
The fields common to the list row and the detail view. Factored out because the two
differ on exactly one field — `sla` is the compact summary on a list row and the full
clock with its segment history on detail — and composing them with `allOf` over a
shared base keeps that difference explicit instead of overriding a parent.

messageCount.description: For a CUSTOMER caller, PUBLIC messages only - the count never reveals that internal notes exist.

openCount.description: null when the user has no agent profile

lastPublicReply.description:
The newest customer-visible message, so a list can say "Support replied 2h
ago" instead of a bare count. `null` until the thread has a public reply
(the opening description is on the ticket, not a message).

fromSupport.description: true when an agent, lead or admin wrote it

sla.description: Compact form. The full segment history is on `GET /tickets/{id}/sla`.

allOf.description:
**A `CUSTOMER` receives a different type entirely** (`TicketCustomerResponse`),
without `priorityRationale`, `analysisStatus`, `latestDraftId`, INTERNAL messages
or the internal SLA detail. Role-based visibility is a separate DTO, not
conditional null-setting — which makes a leak a compile error rather than a
forgotten branch.

sla.description: The full clock shape, against the compact `SlaSummary` on list rows.

fromDraftId.description:
Links this message to the AI draft it came from. Must belong to this ticket and be
`SHOWN`. This is what makes draft acceptance measurable rather than anecdotal.

slaEffect.description:
Present when this message moved a clock. **Written in the same transaction as the
message**, which is what closes the race against the SLA poller: an agent replying
at the instant a breach would fire cannot produce both a first response and a
breach.

force.description: TEAM_LEAD+ only. Reassign a ticket that already has an assignee.

reason.description: Required for `WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER` and `PENDING_THIRD_PARTY` — the two transitions that pause a customer's SLA clock, and therefore the two that need a justification on the record.

TriageSignals.description:
**Observations, not decisions.** There is deliberately no `priority` field here: the
model reports what it sees and a versioned rule set decides what that means. That
split is what makes a wrong priority attributable to either the model or the policy.

extractedEntities.description:
Values may be **PII placeholders** such as `«ORDER_1»` — the real value was
redacted before the text left for the model, so the model never saw it.
Rehydration happens only when rendering for an authorised human.

costMicros.description: Cost in millionths of a rupee. Integers, never floats, for money.

reason.description: Present when `UNAVAILABLE`.

inputs.description: **`fromModel` and `fromSystem` are separate objects on purpose** — that separation is the whole diagnostic value of this endpoint.

confidence.description:
The model's self-reported confidence. Carried here beside the signals
it produced, and deliberately **not** part of `TriageSignals` itself —
it is a property of the call, not an observation about the ticket.

rules.description: Every rule the policy evaluated, **including the ones that did not match** — a rule that silently did not fire is indistinguishable from a rule that does not exist.

Citation.description: `charStart`/`charEnd` locate the claim inside the chunk, so the UI can highlight the exact span rather than the whole document.

DraftClaim.description:
**Rejected claims are returned, not hidden.** The agent can see that the model tried
to invent a refund amount and why it was dropped. Hiding rejections would make the
verification mechanism invisible, and an invisible safety mechanism is an untrusted
one.

coverage.description: Supported claims ÷ total claims. Below 0.80 the draft is suppressed.

assembledText.description: **`null` when suppressed — not a hedged draft.** A confidently wrong answer is worse than no answer.

unresolvedAspects.description: What the knowledge base did **not** answer. The agent's real question is not "what does the KB say" but "what will I have to figure out myself?"

tier.description: A runbook and "someone did this once" should not be weighed the same.

SlaSegment.description:
**Append-only.** A pause closes the open segment and inserts a new one; nothing is
ever updated in place, so there is no counter to drift and the history is the
calculation rather than a log of it.

policyVersion.description: Snapshotted at creation, so tightening a policy does not retroactively breach in-flight tickets.

elapsedBusinessMinutes.description: A `SUM()` over RUNNING segments. Not a stored column.

nextDeadlineAt.description: **`null` while paused**, which is exactly why the poller — `WHERE state = 'RUNNING' AND next_deadline_at <= NOW()` — skips it. The poller is O(due), not O(open).

prediction.description: **Not an LLM output** — a p75 window function over 90 days of history. Faster, cheaper, more accurate and explainable than asking a model.

basis.description: Names the statistic and the sample size, so the number is inspectable rather than magical.

DetectionView.description:
**The deterministic gate's evidence.** `arrivalRateMultiple` against
`gateThresholds.minRateMultiple` is the record of why this was proposed, and it makes
clear that a statistical check — not a model — made that call.

timeToDetectSeconds.description: A headline metric that comes straight out of the schema rather than a stopwatch.

IncidentDetail.description:
The full board-card-plus-everything view. Deliberately **not** composed with `allOf`
over `IncidentSummary` — the detail response has no top-level `timeToDetectSeconds`
(it lives inside `detection`, once) and adds fields a list row has no use for.

titleGeneratedBy.description:
The model that wrote the **title, and nothing else**. `null` means the title
was templated because the LLM was unavailable — and the incident was still
detected, because detection never depended on the model.

detachedTickets.description: Soft-detached links, kept for the audit trail and the evaluation set.

linkConfidence.description: Set for a gate-proposed link; `null` for a manual one.

ConfirmIncidentRequest.description: `pauseResolutionClocks` defaults to `true` when the body is omitted entirely.

firstResponseClocksUnaffected.description:
Count of linked tickets whose first-response clock kept running, because the
customer still deserves an acknowledgement even during an outage.

skipped.description: Ids of linked tickets that could not be auto-resolved; the incident still resolves.

force.description: Bypasses `TOO_MANY_LINKED_TICKETS` for an incident linked to more than 500 tickets.

mimeType.description: **Declared, not trusted.** `/complete` verifies the actual magic bytes.

escalationRungs.description: Percentages of the target at which to escalate. Each rung fires **exactly once**, guaranteed by `uq_escalation_rung` rather than by the poller being careful.

skills.description: Drives routing. Every value must be a valid `Category`.

isDefault.description: At most one per tenant. Clearing the last one is permitted and warned about — unroutable tickets then stay unassigned rather than erroring.

info.title: Papr Memory API
info.description:
API for managing personal memory items with authentication and user-specific data.
## Authentication
This API supports three authentication methods:
- **API Key**: Include your API key in the `X-API-Key` header
  ```
  X-API-Key: <your-api-key>
  ```
- **Session Token**: Include your session token in the `X-Session-Token` header
  ```
  X-Session-Token: <your-session-token>
  ```
- **Bearer Token**: Include your OAuth2 token from Auth0 in the `Authorization` header
  ```
  Authorization: Bearer <token>
  ```
All endpoints require one of these authentication methods.

post.description:
Add a new memory item to the system with size validation and background processing.
    
    **Authentication Required**:
    One of the following authentication methods must be used:
    - Bearer token in `Authorization` header
    - API Key in `X-API-Key` header
    - Session token in `X-Session-Token` header
    
    **Required Headers**:
    - Content-Type: application/json
    - X-Client-Type: (e.g., 'papr_plugin', 'browser_extension')
    
    **Role-Based Memory Categories**:
    - **User memories**: preference, task, goal, facts, context
    - **Assistant memories**: skills, learning
    
    **New Metadata Fields**:
    - `metadata.role`: Optional field to specify who generated the memory (user or assistant)
    - `metadata.category`: Optional field for memory categorization based on role
    - Both fields are stored within metadata at the same level as topics, location, etc.
    
    The API validates content size against MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH environment variable (defaults to 15000 bytes).

post.description:
Search through memories with authentication required.
    
    **Authentication Required**:
    One of the following authentication methods must be used:
    - Bearer token in `Authorization` header
    - API Key in `X-API-Key` header
    - Session token in `X-Session-Token` header
    
    **Custom Schema Support**:
    This endpoint supports both system-defined and custom user-defined node types:
    - **System nodes**: Memory, Person, Company, Project, Task, Insight, Meeting, Opportunity, Code
    - **Custom nodes**: Defined by developers via UserGraphSchema (e.g., Developer, Product, Customer, Function)
    
    When custom schema nodes are returned:
    - Each custom node includes a `schema_id` field referencing the UserGraphSchema
    - The response includes a `schemas_used` array listing all schema IDs used
    - Use `GET /v1/schemas/{schema_id}` to retrieve full schema definitions including:
      - Node type definitions and properties
      - Relationship type definitions and constraints
      - Validation rules and requirements
    
    **Recommended Headers**:
    ```
    Accept-Encoding: gzip
    ```
    
    The API supports response compression for improved performance. Responses larger than 1KB will be automatically compressed when this header is present.
    
    **HIGHLY RECOMMENDED SETTINGS FOR BEST RESULTS:**
    - Set `enable_agentic_graph: true` for intelligent, context-aware search that can understand ambiguous references
    - Use `max_memories: 15-20` for comprehensive memory coverage
    - Use `max_nodes: 10-15` for comprehensive graph entity relationships
    
    **Agentic Graph Benefits:**
    When enabled, the system can understand vague references by first identifying specific entities from your memory graph, then performing targeted searches. For example:
    - "customer feedback" → identifies your customers first, then finds their specific feedback
    - "project issues" → identifies your projects first, then finds related issues
    - "team meeting notes" → identifies your team members first, then finds meeting notes
    - "code functions" → identifies your functions first, then finds related code
    
    **Role-Based Memory Filtering:**
    Filter memories by role and category using metadata fields:
    - `metadata.role`: Filter by "user" or "assistant" 
    - `metadata.category`: Filter by category (user: preference, task, goal, facts, context | assistant: skills, learning)
    
    **User Resolution Precedence:**
    - If both user_id and external_user_id are provided, user_id takes precedence.
    - If only external_user_id is provided, it will be resolved to the internal user.
    - If neither is provided, the authenticated user is used.

post.description:
Submit feedback on search results to help improve model performance.
    
    This endpoint allows developers to provide feedback on:
    - Overall answer quality (thumbs up/down, ratings)
    - Specific memory relevance and accuracy
    - User engagement signals (copy, save, create document actions)
    - Corrections and improvements
    
    The feedback is used to train and improve:
    - Router model tier predictions
    - Memory retrieval ranking
    - Answer generation quality
    - Agentic graph search performance
    
    **Authentication Required**:
    One of the following authentication methods must be used:
    - Bearer token in `Authorization` header
    - API Key in `X-API-Key` header
    - Session token in `X-Session-Token` header
    
    **Required Headers**:
    - Content-Type: application/json
    - X-Client-Type: (e.g., 'papr_plugin', 'browser_extension')

post.description:
Store a chat message and queue it for AI analysis and memory creation.
    
    **Authentication Required**: Bearer token, API key, or session token
    
    **Processing Control**:
    - Set `process_messages: true` (default) to enable full AI analysis and memory creation
    - Set `process_messages: false` to store messages only without processing into memories
    
    **Processing Flow** (when process_messages=true):
    1. Message is immediately stored in PostMessage class
    2. Background processing analyzes the message for memory-worthiness
    3. If worthy, creates a memory with appropriate role-based categorization
    4. Links the message to the created memory
    
    **Role-Based Categories**:
    - **User messages**: preference, task, goal, facts, context
    - **Assistant messages**: skills, learning
    
    **Session Management**:
    - `sessionId` is required to group related messages
    - Use the same `sessionId` for an entire conversation
    - Retrieve conversation history using GET /messages/sessions/{sessionId}

get.description:
OAuth2 login endpoint. Initiates the OAuth2 authorization code flow.
    
    **Query Parameters:**
    - `redirect_uri`: The URI to redirect to after authentication (required)
    - `state`: A random string for CSRF protection (optional but recommended)
    
    **Flow:**
    1. Client redirects user to this endpoint with `redirect_uri` and `state`
    2. This endpoint redirects user to Auth0 for authentication
    3. After authentication, Auth0 redirects to `/callback` with authorization code
    4. `/callback` redirects back to the original `redirect_uri` with code and state
    
    **Example:**
    ```
    GET /login?redirect_uri=https://chat.openai.com&state=abc123
    ```

500.description: Internal server error

get.description:
OAuth2 callback endpoint. Processes the authorization code from Auth0.
    
    **Query Parameters:**
    - `code`: Authorization code from Auth0 (required)
    - `state`: State parameter for CSRF protection (required)
    
    **Flow:**
    1. Auth0 redirects to this endpoint after successful authentication
    2. This endpoint validates the authorization code and state
    3. Redirects back to the original `redirect_uri` with code and state
    4. Client can then exchange the code for tokens at `/token` endpoint
    
    **Security:**
    - Validates state parameter to prevent CSRF attacks
    - Checks authorization code expiration
    - Cleans up session data after processing

400.description: Bad request - missing code or state

500.description: Internal server error

post.description:
OAuth2 token endpoint. Exchanges authorization code for access tokens.
    
    **Request Body (JSON or Form):**
    - `grant_type`: OAuth2 grant type - "authorization_code" or "refresh_token" (required)
    - `code`: Authorization code from OAuth2 callback (required for authorization_code grant)
    - `redirect_uri`: Redirect URI used in authorization (required for authorization_code grant)
    - `client_type`: Client type - "papr_plugin" or "browser_extension" (optional, default: papr_plugin)
    - `refresh_token`: Refresh token for token refresh (required for refresh_token grant)
    
    **Response:**
    - `access_token`: OAuth2 access token for API authentication
    - `token_type`: Token type (Bearer)
    - `expires_in`: Token expiration time in seconds
    - `refresh_token`: Refresh token for getting new access tokens
    - `scope`: OAuth2 scopes granted
    - `user_id`: User ID from Auth0
    
    **Example Request:**
    ```json
    {
        "grant_type": "authorization_code",
        "code": "abc123...",
        "redirect_uri": "https://chat.openai.com",
        "client_type": "papr_plugin"
    }
    ```

    X-Client-Type: papr_plugin
    ```

get.description:
OAuth2 logout endpoint. Logs out the user from Auth0 and redirects to specified URL.
    
    **Query Parameters:**
    - `returnTo`: URL to redirect to after logout (optional, default: extension logout page)
    - `client_type`: Client type for determining Auth0 client ID (optional, default: papr_plugin)
    
    **Flow:**
    1. Client redirects user to this endpoint
    2. This endpoint redirects to Auth0 logout URL
    3. Auth0 logs out the user and redirects to the specified return URL
    
    **Example:**
    ```
    GET /logout?returnTo=https://chat.openai.com
    ```
    
    **Note:** This endpoint initiates the logout process. The actual logout completion happens on Auth0's side.

info.title: Survey Engine MVP API
info.description:
Comprehensive API contract for the Survey Engine MVP.

This specification is written for product, implementation, and integration teams.
Every endpoint description intentionally includes:
1) why the endpoint is needed,
2) what the endpoint does,
3) how the endpoint works inside the platform lifecycle.

Security model summary:
- Admin APIs accept engine-issued JWT via HttpOnly access_token cookie (primary) or Bearer header (fallback).
- Headless clients can use explicit token-mode auth endpoints under /api/v1/admin/auth/token/*.
- Admin sessions are maintained with refresh-token cookie rotation.
- Browser cookie mode exposes CSRF bootstrap endpoint at /api/v1/admin/auth/csrf.
- Responder submission endpoint is public at transport level, but private campaigns enforce tenant-scoped responder authentication in business logic.
