get.summary: Authorization endpoint — authorization code flow with PKCE
get.description: Takes `response_type=code`, `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope`, `state`, `nonce`, `code_challenge` and `code_challenge_method=S256`, and answers 302 to the registered redirect URI with a single-use code that expires in 60 seconds. It requires a bearer access token: this provider has no login page, so the account signs in through the credential endpoints first — SPEC-044, the owner's answer A. An unknown client or an unregistered redirect URI answers 400 without redirecting, because sending an error to a URI nobody registered is the open redirect the registry exists to prevent.

302.description: Found

post.summary: Token endpoint — code exchange and refresh
post.description: Form-encoded, as RFC 6749 requires. With `grant_type=authorization_code` it takes `code`, `code_verifier`, `client_id` and `redirect_uri`, spends the code once, and answers an access token, an ID token and a refresh token. With `grant_type=refresh_token` it takes `refresh_token` and rotates the session, which revokes the whole family if a spent token is presented. There is no `grant_type=password`: OAuth 2.1 removes it. Errors are RFC 6749 §5.2 objects, not ProblemDetails.

get.description: The claims the session's grant allows — OpenID Connect Core 1.0 §5.3. `sub` always; `email` and `email_verified` when the `email` scope was granted; `name` when `profile` was. A session opened by the credential endpoints granted no scope and receives all of them, because the caller is the account's own client. The subject comes from the validated token and never from a parameter.

post.description: Form-encoded `token`, with an optional `token_type_hint` — RFC 7009. Revoking a refresh token ends its whole session: every token descended from the same sign-in stops rotating. An unknown or already-revoked token answers 200 as well, so the endpoint is not an oracle for which tokens exist. `token_type_hint=access_token` answers 400 `unsupported_token_type`, because a short-lived signed access token is not revocable here and a 200 would say otherwise.

get.description: What this provider offers. Only endpoints that answer are listed: a client reading this document may assume every URL in it exists.
The public half of every key a token from this API may carry: the current one, and the outgoing one during a rotation overlap. Private material never appears here.
Returns 200 while the process is serving. Touches no dependency.
Returns 200 when every dependency is reachable, 503 when one is not.

post.description: Takes the current password as proof and replaces it. Every other session the account holds is revoked; the caller's own stays alive, because it is the session that just proved it holds the new credential. A wrong current password is 422, not 401: the token is fine.

get.summary: List the devices the caller has been given control of
get.description: The delegation seen from the other side: what somebody else handed me, not what I handed out.

post.description: Accepts the registration and answers 202 whether or not the address is already registered. A 409 here would tell an anonymous caller who holds an account; the mailbox tells the real user what happened.

202.description: Accepted

post.description: Spends a verification credential exactly once and marks the address verified. Send either `token`, from the link, or `email` with the six-character `code` from the message. A wrong code costs one of five attempts against that message, after which it is spent whatever is typed. The description says nothing about what separates 400 from 410 for a given credential, because that is the caller's business only when they hold it.

post.summary: Ask for another email verification link
post.description: Answers 202 for any address that is a valid address. Whether a mail follows is not stated and cannot be inferred from the response: a distinct answer here would tell an anonymous caller which addresses hold a registered or confirmed account.

202.description: Accepted

post.description: Exchanges an address and a password for a token pair. Every failure — unknown address, wrong password, unverified account — answers the same bodiless 401, and the unknown-address path spends the same hashing work as the others, so the response cannot be timed either.

get.description: Lists the caller's live sessions, newest first, each with the platform, device and app version that started it so a session can be recognised. No token and no digest is returned: the list exists to be read, not to be replayed.

post.description: Spends a refresh token exactly once and returns a rotated pair. Presenting an already-rotated token revokes the whole family and answers 401: that is the session-theft detector, and it answers exactly as an unknown or expired token does.

post.summary: Ask for a password reset link
post.description: Answers 202 for any address that is a valid address. Whether a mail follows is not stated and cannot be inferred from the response: a distinct answer here would tell an anonymous caller which addresses hold an account.

202.description: Accepted

post.description: Takes either the token from the reset link or the address and the six-character code from the same mail, spends it exactly once, replaces the password and revokes every refresh token the account holds, so a password change ends every session opened with the old one. Five wrong codes spend the row. An access token issued moments earlier stays valid until it expires; that window is the 15 minutes the session design fixes. A 422 describes the new password only, never the credential.

delete.description: Revokes the refresh-token family this access token belongs to, named by its sid claim, so no token from this session can be rotated again. The access token already issued stays valid until it expires — at most 15 minutes and 30 seconds — which is the accepted window in the threat register rather than an oversight.

Revokes one named session of the calling account. An unknown id, one already ended and one belonging to another account all answer 404, because a distinct answer would confirm that another account's session exists.

post.description: Exchanges an authorization code for a token pair. The code is exchanged by this API with the client secret, never by the client — ADR-0008. An account is created the first time an identity signs in, and it has no password until the owner sets one through the reset flow.

get.description: The caller's own links, oldest first. No route reads anybody else's.

post.summary: Link a provider to this account
post.description: The same acquisition as signing in, deliberately: linking an identity the caller cannot prove they hold would let anyone attach their provider account to somebody else's.

409.description: Conflict

delete.description: Refused with 409 when it is the account's only way in: an account with no password and one link would become one nobody can reach, including its owner.

409.description: Conflict

get.description: Returns every profile field with the visibility tier that governs it, plus the caller's music preferences. The owner is the one reader who sees every tier; what another user sees is projected per field, which is a different endpoint.

patch.description: Updates any subset of the profile. Each field carries its value and its visibility tier in the same object, so a field cannot exist without a tier — a value with no tier is 422, never a silent default to public. An absent field is left untouched; sending a null value with a tier clears it.

put.description: Replaces the whole preference set, genres and artists. Preferences are private to their owner and carry no visibility tier of their own. Both lists are bounded: an unbounded array behind an authenticated endpoint is unrestricted resource consumption.

get.description: Lists the caller's friends, newest first, paged. A friendship is symmetric: both parties see each other here, and neither can see it without the other.

delete.description: Ends the friendship for both sides at once, and clears the request rows between the pair so they may befriend again. Answers 404 when there is no friendship to end.

get.description: Lists pending requests in one direction: incoming are the ones addressed to the caller, outgoing the ones the caller sent. The direction is required, because the two screens that show these lists show one each.

post.description: Creates a pending request. Answers 409 when the pair are already friends, when a request is already pending in either direction, or when the caller asks themselves; 404 when no such account exists. A crossing request is not auto-accepted: nobody becomes a friend without accepting.

409.description: Conflict

patch.summary: Accept or decline a friend request
patch.description: Only the recipient may answer. Accepting creates the friendship in the same transaction that marks the request accepted, so twenty simultaneous accepts produce one friendship. An unknown request, one already answered and one addressed to somebody else all answer 404.

delete.summary: Withdraw a friend request you sent
delete.description: Only the sender may withdraw; a recipient declines instead, which is a different verb and a different row state. The row is deleted rather than marked, so the pair may try again.

get.description: Matches a case-insensitive prefix of the display name, paged with a capped size. The display name is the only field searched: matching a profile field would let a stranger confirm a friends-only value by probing for it. A blank query returns nothing rather than everybody.

Returns the profile projected per field against the caller's relationship to its owner: self, friend or stranger. A field the caller may not see is absent from the body and is never read from the database, so a caller cannot tell a hidden field from an empty one. An account that does not exist answers the same sparse shape as one whose owner hid everything, so asking does not confirm existence.

post.description: The caller owns it. A playlist may be Everyone or InvitedOnly; LocationAndTimeRestricted is 422, because that licence belongs to an event and nothing checks a geofence on a playlist.

get.description: One scope at a time: mine, shared with me, or public. Paged with a capped size. A private playlist the caller is not named on never appears in any scope.
Returns the playlist with an ETag the client sends back as If-Match when it edits. A playlist the caller may not see answers 404, never 403, because 403 would confirm it exists.

patch.description: Requires If-Match carrying the ETag the client last read. A stale or absent token answers 412 and changes nothing: two clients editing at once is the failure this guard exists for.

412.description: Precondition Failed

delete.description: A soft delete, owner only: the row is stamped deleted and disappears from every read. Its audit trail keeps pointing at something that exists.

put.summary: Set a playlist's visibility and licence
put.description: Owner only: a collaborator who may edit the contents does not decide who may see them.

get.summary: List who is named on a playlist
get.description: Anybody who may see the playlist may see who is named on it. A caller who may not see the playlist answers 404, not an empty list, because an empty list would confirm it exists.

post.description: Owner only. 409 when they are already named, and when the owner names themselves — they already hold every right a collaborator grant could give.

409.description: Conflict

delete.description: Owner only. 404 when there is no such grant on a playlist this caller owns.

get.summary: List a playlist's tracks in order
get.description: Anybody who may see the playlist may see its tracks. The response carries the ETag the client sends back as If-Match when it adds, moves or removes one. A caller who may not see the playlist answers 404, not an empty list, because an empty list would confirm it exists.

post.summary: Add a track to a playlist
post.description: Requires If-Match carrying the ETag of the track list the client last read. Appends by default; atHead or afterTrackId names a position. A playlist already holding its maximum number of tracks answers 409. The same video may appear twice: a playlist that plays a track twice is a playlist, not an error.

409.description: Conflict

412.description: Precondition Failed

patch.summary: Move a track within a playlist
patch.description: Exactly one of afterTrackId or beforeTrackId. Requires If-Match: when two clients reorder the same list at once exactly one is applied and the other is told 412 and reloads, which is the whole point of versioning a collection.

412.description: Precondition Failed

delete.summary: Remove a track from a playlist
delete.description: Requires If-Match. Removing leaves the remaining order untouched: positions are sparse, so the hole costs nothing and no other row is rewritten.

412.description: Precondition Failed

post.description: The caller owns it. The window is two UTC instants and the end must be after the start. A LocationAndTimeRestricted licence must name the presence proof it requires, and a geofence proof must carry a centre and a radius, or the answer is 422.

get.description: One scope at a time: mine, the ones I was invited to, or public. Paged with a capped size. A private event the caller was not invited to appears in none of them.
Returns the event with an ETag the client sends back as If-Match when it edits. An event the caller may not see answers 404, never 403, because 403 would confirm it exists.

patch.description: Owner only, and requires If-Match carrying the ETag the client last read. A stale or absent token answers 412 and changes nothing.

412.description: Precondition Failed

delete.description: A soft delete, owner only: the row is stamped deleted and disappears from every read, so its audit trail keeps pointing at something that exists.

put.summary: Set an event's visibility, licence and presence policy
put.description: Owner only. The same rules creation applies: an event cannot become a LocationAndTimeRestricted event with nothing configured to check.

get.description: Owner only. Who else was invited to a private event is not a participant's business, and an empty list for a non-owner would still confirm the event exists — so the answer is 404.

post.description: Owner only. A duplicate is 409, decided by the unique index rather than by a read-then-write check. Inviting the owner is also 409: they already hold the strongest grant.

409.description: Conflict

delete.description: Owner only. The gate is read live on every request, so the invitee loses access on their next call rather than on their next sign-in.

post.description: Any authenticated caller on a public event, an invitee on a private one. This is a roster and never a precondition: voting does not require it.

409.description: Conflict

delete.description: `current` rather than a user id: the only attendance a caller may remove is their own.

get.description: Anybody who may see the event may see its queue. Ordered by vote count and then by when each track was suggested, so the order is total and stable. Each row says whether the caller voted, and the count is read from the vote rows rather than from a stored counter.

post.summary: Suggest a track for an event
post.description: Behind the licence gate: who may suggest is who may vote. The same video twice is 409, because two rows would split its votes between two queue entries.

409.description: Conflict

delete.description: The suggester's or the event owner's, and nobody else's. Its votes go with it: a vote is a vote for that suggestion, and orphaned rows would leave a count that counts nothing.

put.description: Idempotent: 201 the first time and 200 after, including when a concurrent request wrote the vote first — the unique index is the arbiter. On a LocationAndTimeRestricted event the body carries presence, and a missing or failed proof is 422. The coordinate is compared and discarded; it is never stored and never logged.

delete.description: The caller's own vote and no other. No presence proof is asked for: leaving the venue is not a reason to be stuck having voted, and a withdrawal lowers a count rather than raising one.

post.description: Owner only, and rate limited per account. The code is returned once and stored only as a SHA-256 digest; it is single-use per account, so one code works for a whole room exactly once each.

get.summary: Read what an event is playing
get.description: Anybody who may see the event may see what it is playing, which is the rule GET /playback-sessions/{sessionId} already applies — this route is for the guest who has the event and not the session id. The answer carries nowPlayingStartedAtUtc, so a guest arriving mid-track starts from the right second rather than from the beginning, and serverNowUtc, so they can correct for their own clock. An event with nothing playing, and an event the caller may not see, both answer 404. When two devices are playing one event, the newest live session answers.

post.description: Takes no body: the platform, the model and the app version come from the mandatory client headers. Registering the same device twice is 409, where the same device means the same owner, platform and model — a phone that updates its app is the same phone.

409.description: Conflict

get.description: Only the caller's. The route takes no account id, because a route that accepted one would be a route somebody would eventually pass somebody else's.

delete.summary: Remove one of the caller's devices
delete.description: Owner only. Another account's device answers 404, never 403, because 403 would confirm it exists.

get.description: The owner or the current controller may ask; anybody else gets 404. With no grant the controller is the owner. The response carries the ETag a claim sends back as If-Match.

put.summary: Hand playback control to a friend
put.description: Owner only, and requires If-Match. The grantee must be a friend of the owner, or the answer is 422. Two simultaneous claims: one 200, one 412 — the loser loses visibly, because two clients each believing they hold one device is the bug.

412.description: Precondition Failed

delete.summary: Return a device to its owner's control
delete.description: The owner's revoke and the controller's release are the same route and the same effect. A device already under owner control answers 404: there was no grant to release.

get.summary: Read what a device is playing
get.description: The device's owner or its current controller: the people who could change what it plays are the people entitled to know what it is playing. A device that is not playing answers 404.
The only route that can reach YouTube's expensive search call, so it is rate limited per account and its results are cached. A repeated query inside the cache window costs no quota at all.

Prefers both cache levels, then one cheap metadata call. A video the catalog does not know is 404, and so is a malformed id — the contract lists no 422 here, and one answer for both keeps the route from saying which ids are well formed. A catalog that cannot answer at all is 503.

post.summary: Start playing a source on a device
post.description: The device's owner starts playback, on a source they may see. The server picks what plays first. A device already playing answers 409: it holds at most one live session.

409.description: Conflict

get.description: Anybody who may see the source may see what it is playing, with the ETag a command sends back as If-Match. A caller who may not see the source answers 404.

patch.description: The one route where the client chooses what plays, so it is guarded and bounded: the controller may jump, and only to an item of the source already playing.

412.description: Precondition Failed

delete.description: The device's owner stops it: a delegate steers what plays and does not get to switch the speaker off. The row is stamped ended rather than deleted, and the device may start again.

post.description: The controller's route. The server picks the next item — highest vote count for an event, next position for a playlist. `expectedNowPlayingId` makes a retry harmless: a stale expectation returns the current state rather than skipping a second track. A stale If-Match is 412. Nothing left to play ends the session and answers 409.

409.description: Conflict

412.description: Precondition Failed

put.summary: Report where the playing device is
put.description: The controller's route, as the jump is: only the thing playing the music can honestly say where it is. The server stamps its own clock on the report and broadcasts PlaybackPositionChanged, so a guest can seek to the same second. A report naming a track that is no longer playing is discarded — it was in flight while the session advanced, and acting on it would drag every listener backwards. An ended session, and a caller who may not command this one, both answer 404. The session's own ETag is untouched: a report is not a move, and a controller's If-Match keeps working. One report per second per session; above that is 429.

info.title: AthletOS API
info.description: A governor for athletes who already train.

get.summary: The public keys access tokens are signed with.
get.description:
Public and unauthenticated by definition: it carries only public keys, and a
verifier needs it before it holds any credential to authenticate with.

200.description: The active JSON Web Key Set

get.summary: Liveness probe — answers as long as the process is serving requests.

Readiness probe — additionally verifies the database is reachable, so an
orchestrator does not route traffic to an instance that cannot serve it.

500.description: A dependency is unreachable

put.summary: Replaces the athlete's maxes with exactly what is sent.
put.description:
A `PUT` of the whole document, not a patch: what the client holds is one
form, and a partial upsert would leave "clear the max I entered by mistake"
with no representation at all. A key absent from the body is therefore a key
deleted, and the whole thing is one transaction so a half-applied form is not
a state the athlete can end up in.

Removing a max cannot break a program already running. A prescriptive block
snapshots the maxes it was started from (D-03) and an adaptive one keeps its
training max in `State`, so neither reads this table again after enrolment —
which is also why editing a number here does not retroactively rewrite
sessions the athlete has already been shown (D-07).

422.description: An unknown exercise key or an implausible weight

post.summary: Exchanges an athlete's email and password for a token pair.

429.description: Too many consecutive failures for this address; `Retry-After` says how long to wait (ADR-0017)

post.summary:
Ends the session the refresh token belongs to, and revokes the access token
presented alongside it.
post.description:
Both credentials are revoked because revoking only the refresh token leaves
the caller holding a bearer token that keeps working for up to its full
lifetime after they pressed "sign out". The access token's `jti` goes on the
denylist (`auth::denylist`), which the authenticated extractor already
consults as part of the query it was making anyway.

Both are optional, and the sensible behaviours differ:

* refresh token only — the ordinary BFF logout. The session dies; any access
  token already handed out lives until its `exp`, because nothing links an
  access token to a refresh family and inventing that link would mean
  storing every access token, which is precisely what ADR-0003 avoids. The
  15-minute ceiling is the residual exposure, and it is why the access token
  should be sent too.
* access token only — a client that never held a refresh token, or lost it.
  The token presented is revoked immediately.

Idempotent, and it still never reveals whether either credential existed: an
attacker holding a stolen token must not learn anything by logging it out.
A request carrying neither credential is a malformed request, not a silent
success, and is the one case that is refused.

422.description: Neither a refresh token nor an access token was presented

get.summary:
The athlete the presented access token identifies. Also the smallest
possible proof that the extractor works.

post.summary: Exchanges a refresh token for a new pair, invalidating the one presented.
post.description:
Presenting a token that was already exchanged revokes every token in its
family — see `auth::refresh` for why.

401.description: The refresh token is unknown, spent, expired or revoked

post.summary: Creates an athlete and signs them straight in.
post.description:
Registration is open (D-02). The inherited design was invitation-only, with a
`bootstrap` binary that refused to run twice; that is the wrong shape for a
product whose unit is one athlete.

Three things about this handler are deliberate.

**It answers 409 when the address is taken**, which is an account
enumeration oracle, and there is no way to build an open registration
endpoint without one: the alternative — accept everything and say "check your
email" — requires mail, and v1 has no SMTP by decision (D-02, D-14). Saying
so plainly is better than a refusal the athlete cannot act on. The detail
text is neutral about *why*, so it reads the same to whoever receives it.

**The password is checked before it is hashed and before the row exists.**
The policy needs the address and the name as context — they are the first two
things anyone guessing this account tries — so validation has to run in this
order rather than in the order the fields arrive.

**It is not throttled.** `auth::throttle` exists to bound guessing against an
address that already has an account (SP 800-63B-4 §3.2.2), and there is
nothing here to guess. What does bound this endpoint is the Argon2 hash it
spends before touching the database, including on a duplicate address.

201.description: The account exists and is signed in

409.description: An account already uses that address

422.description: The address, name or password was refused

get.summary: Every program this athlete has run, current one first.
get.description:
This is how a client that has been reloaded finds its way back: the enrolment
id it needs for `next-session` and for `POST /v1/workouts` is not something it
can derive, and a BFF cookie holding it would be a second source of truth for
a fact the database already knows.

Both a `status` filter and an active-first ordering, which is not
belt-and-braces. The filter is what a client asking "what am I running"
should send. The ordering is what keeps the *unfiltered* call — "programs
I've run", the D-13 reading — from making the client sort to find the live
one. A default order that answers the common question is worth more than one
that is merely chronological, and it costs a boolean in the `order by`.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description:
One of `active`, `finished` or `abandoned`. Omitted returns all of them.

A `String` parsed by hand rather than the `EnrollmentStatus` enum
deserialized straight from the query string. Two reasons: the refusal can
then name the legal values, where a deserializer rejection is a bare 400
with none of the RFC 9457 shape the rest of this API answers in; and a
query parameter typed as a closed vocabulary is a parameter that cannot
grow, which is the one thing `/v1` may never do (D-12).

422.description: `status` is not one of the three

post.summary: Starts a program for the authenticated athlete.
post.description:
The engine validates: `start()` derives the whole block (or, for an adaptive
program, every training max) purely so that a missing max fails here, at
enrolment, rather than as a zero-kilo prescription on day one of week one.
That refusal reaches the caller as a 422 naming the exercise key — see the
`ProgramError` conversion in `crate::error`.

Nothing stops an athlete holding several enrolments at once, including in the
same program. The schema's active-enrolment index is deliberately not unique:
running a squat block and a bench block side by side is a product question
nobody has answered yet, and a constraint would answer it by accident.

422.description: The athlete has not entered a max this program needs

Reads adjustments for an enrolment owned by the authenticated athlete.

history and settings screens merely because the block ended.

The request first lands as generic JSON so a fractional number can be
translated into this API's RFC 9457 422 response. Extracting the DTO

get.summary: What the athlete is doing next. **Read-only** (D-08).
get.description:
No row is written, no timer starts, and no state moves. `started_at` is
stamped on commit, which happens on the phone and arrives later as a
`POST /v1/workouts` — this endpoint exists precisely so that looking is free.
If this handler ever acquires a write, the distinction D-08 is built on has
been lost. It acquired a second *read* in phase 5, for the pace projection,
and that is the line: reads are what "free" means.

anybody's data, but opening an endpoint later is additive and closing one is

Deliberately the same shape the list returns rather than a richer one. A
detail view that showed the actual prescribed sessions would have to derive
them from the athlete's maxes, which is what enrolling is for — and showing a
preview built from maxes the athlete has not entered would mean inventing

parameters.description: The program's registry key

get.summary: Where a year of training went.
get.description:
# One round trip, and nothing stored

Four queries, no writes, and no table behind any of it (D-13, amended). The
estimate is [`athletos_training::estimate`] over stored sets, load and drift
are sums over the same rows, the training max is `readout()` applied to the
`state_before` [`crate::advances`] already records, and the intervals come
off [`crate::timing`]'s own walk. Every figure here is implied by rows that
exist for other reasons, which is exactly why a metrics table was declined:
a stored total is a second copy of an arithmetic fact, and the day it
disagrees with the rows there is no way to tell which one is wrong.

# The scope, and the index that does not serve it

`workouts` has no `athlete_id`, so ownership arrives through the join on
`enrollments` in all four queries — the same shape, and the same accepted
cost, that [`crate::routes::workouts::history`] documents at length. The
window bounds it: this is one person's twelve months, which is hundreds of
sessions and low thousands of sets at the volume this product is designed
for.

# A deviation from the spec: fixed, not overridable

The spec calls the window "twelve months by default, overridable". This
ships the default and not the override — no query parameter — because
building one was out of scope for this pass. What it does carry is
[`ProgressView::window_months`], so a client rendering `overall.sessions`
can caption it correctly without knowing [`WINDOW_MONTHS`] exists. That
closes the half of the gap that would otherwise force a client to hardcode
a server-side constant (D-11); it does not close the other half, and an
athlete cannot yet ask this endpoint for eighteen months instead of twelve.

get.summary: Everything the athlete has logged, newest first.
get.description:
# Pagination, and the index that does not exist

Offset and limit, not a keyset cursor. Keyset is the stabler construction and
it is not the one that fits here: the sort key would have to be
`(started_at, id)` to break ties, and the only index over `workouts` is
`(enrollment_id, started_at desc)`, which carries neither `athlete_id` nor
`id`. So keyset would buy no index advantage and would trade one form of
drift for an opaque cursor. The drift offset does have is real and small: a
workout submitted while the athlete is paging shifts rows by one, which in a
"load more" list read by one person is a repeated or skipped row, not a wrong
answer.

The honest cost of the unfiltered call is that Postgres materialises and
sorts one athlete's *entire* workout history per page. `workouts` has no
`athlete_id`, so the scope comes through a join and no index over `workouts`
can answer the ordering — this is a sort, and it is bounded by how many
sessions one person has logged. At the hundreds this is designed for that
costs nothing worth measuring. If it ever does, the fix is to denormalise
`athlete_id` onto `workouts` with an index on `(athlete_id, started_at
desc)`; that is an additive migration, and adding the column now — untested,
unmeasured, and duplicating a fact `enrollments` already owns — is exactly
the speculative move the schema's own comments argue against.

Supplying `enrollment_id` sidesteps all of it: that query is one walk of the
existing index, in order, and stops at the limit.

parameters.name: enrollment_id
parameters.description:
Only this enrolment's workouts — "how did that block go".

Worth having beyond convenience: with it supplied the query is one walk
of `workouts_enrollment_id_idx (enrollment_id, started_at desc)` and
needs no sort at all, which the athlete-wide query cannot manage.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Rows per page. Defaults to 25, clamped to 100.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Rows to skip. Defaults to 0.

200.description: A page of history, newest first

post.summary: Records a finished session and advances the program exactly once.

200.description: A retry of a submit already accepted; nothing moved

404.description: No such enrolment belongs to this athlete

409.description: The enrolment has nothing left to log, or the id is already used by another enrolment

413.description: Too many sets in one submission

get.summary: One workout and every set of it.
get.description:
A separate endpoint rather than an `?include=sets` flag on the list, for the
interaction it serves: expand-on-tap opens one row at a time, and an include
flag would fetch the sets for a whole page whether or not anything was
expanded — around a thousand rows to render twenty-five dates, on a phone.
A submitted workout is also immutable, so this response can be cached hard by
the client where a list response cannot. And the choice is not final in the
direction that matters: an `include` flag can be added later if the extra
round trip ever hurts, whereas a field cannot be taken back out of the list
(D-12).

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The workout's id — the one the client minted

200.description: The workout, with every set as logged

404.description: No such workout belongs to this athlete

Actual work and estimates across all sources
Prepared session; clock has not started

AthleteProgress.description:
The whole screen, in one round trip.

# Why the component is called `AthleteProgress`

`routes::enrollments::ProgressView` — sessions completed out of a block —
has been shipping under the component name `ProgressView` since the first
release, and utoipa names a component after the type's last path segment.
Registering a second `ProgressView` does not collide loudly; it overwrites,
and the generated TypeScript would silently start describing this screen
wherever an enrolment's `progress` field is read. D-12 forbids changing what
an existing `/v1` field means, so the older name stays with the older type
and the newcomer takes an alias. The Rust name is unchanged and the JSON on
the wire is unaffected: this renames a schema, not a field.

window_months.description:
How many months of history `lifts`, `sessions` and `overall` cover —
[`WINDOW_MONTHS`], carried onto the wire. `bests` is the one exception
and is not bounded by it (see that function). Named rather than left
implicit so a client can caption `overall`'s `sessions` figure as
"Sessions (last N months)" without hardcoding a number only the server
knows — the same reason `indicators_from`'s doc comment gives for why
the client is never told what a metric means beyond its `unit` (D-11).

AuthenticatedAthlete.description:
A verified athlete.

Deliberately just the id: v1 has one athlete per account and no teams
(D-14), so there is nothing else an authorization decision needs. Coaching
arrives in v2 as a coach↔athlete relation, which is a different shape from
the generic team roles this replaced — so there is nothing here to keep
warm for it either.

Best.description:
One cell of the rep-max grid: the heaviest weight lifted for **at least**
`reps` reps, and the set it came from.

actual_reps.description: What was actually done at that weight — always at least `reps`.

reps.description: The bucket, not the reps performed.

BlockView.description: One exercise and everything prescribed for it in this session.

cues.description:
How to do it, from the compiled exercise registry.

Resolved here rather than stored with the session, so a corrected cue
reaches every session including ones already logged. The engine's `Block`
deliberately carries only the key for exactly that reason; a PWA cannot
call into the registry itself, so the key is resolved at read time on
this side of the wire instead.

is_primary.description: A competition lift or a close variant, as opposed to accessory work.

token.description: Returned once; only its SHA-256 digest is stored.

CutReason.description: The four answers to the one question asked when a session ends early (D-08).

DriftReason.description:
Why a set was lifted at something other than the prescribed weight (D-07).

Optional in every direction. The chips that produce it are unselected by
default, no tap is a valid answer, and nothing blocks — a default would
answer the question on the athlete's behalf and land a claim nobody made in
the one signal this product exists to read.

Enrollment.description: One athlete's run of one program.

ended_at.description:
When the block ended, and `null` for exactly as long as `status` is
`active` — the schema will not have it any other way.

readout.description:
The numbers this enrolment is prescribing from, **read-only** (D-04).

Served here rather than on `next-session` because of who asks. The
question is "what is my program working from", which the maxes screen asks
about *every* active program at once — on `next-session` that would be one
request per enrolment, and each of them would also compute a prescription
and a pace projection that nobody asked for. It would also go missing at
the moment it is most interesting: `next-session` answers 409 once a block
is finished, and where a training max ended up is exactly what an athlete
looks at when a program ends.

It costs nothing to put here. `progress` already runs the program over the
state this row carries; this runs it once more over the same bytes, with
no extra query.

EnrollmentList.description:
Every enrolment the athlete has ever held.

An object rather than a bare array, so a cursor or a count can be added
without changing the type of the response (D-12).

Deliberately unpaginated, unlike the workout history. An enrolment is created
by a deliberate human act — you press a button to start a program — so the
list is bounded by how many programs someone chooses to run, which is a
number in the tens over a lifetime. Workouts grow with every session and are
paginated for that reason.

EstimateChange.description: First-to-latest estimated-strength change over the trend window.

percent.description: Absent when the first estimate is zero: no finite percentage exists.

ExerciseAdjustments.description: The canonical non-zero adjustments stored for one enrolment.

ExerciseCatalogue.description:
Every exercise the compiled-in programs know about.

An object rather than a bare array, so this can grow a cursor or a filter
without changing the type of the response (D-12).

ExerciseSpend.description: One exercise's share of the session.

counted_sets.description:
How many of this exercise's sets contributed an interval. Less than the
number of sets performed when stamps were missing or discarded, which is
what stops `seconds` being read as authoritative when it is not.

seconds.description:
Summed intervals for every set of this exercise that had a believable
one. Excludes the lead-in even for the first exercise.

ExerciseSummary.description: One exercise, as a client renders it in a list.

is_primary.description:
A competition lift or a close variant, as opposed to accessory work.

Carried so a picker can put the lifts an athlete is likely to track a max
for at the top, without a client holding its own opinion about which
those are.

key.description: Stable key. This is what the maxes document is keyed by.

Indicator.description:
One card. Every figure on the screen is one of these, so the client has one
component and a new metric touches no client code.

IntervalSpread.description: The shape of one session's intervals: fastest, typical, slowest.

average_seconds.description:
Arithmetic mean over the same believable answer-to-answer intervals as
the other figures. Kept alongside the median so clients can choose the
shape that best answers their question without restating the filter.

discarded.description:
Intervals thrown away as impossible, so a screen showing these figures
can say why they account for less than the wall clock.

median_seconds.description:
Median, not mean. One interval spent talking to somebody moves a mean
of twelve by a minute, and the tail of this distribution is not signal —
the same rule, and the same reason, as [`crate::pace`].

Jwk.description: An Ed25519 public key as an OKP JWK (RFC 8037).

alg.description: Algorithm the key is used with; always `EdDSA`.

crv.description: Curve; always `Ed25519`.

kid.description: Key id, matching the `kid` header of tokens signed with it.

kty.description: Key type; always `OKP` for Ed25519.

x.description: The 32-byte public key, base64url-encoded without padding.

oneOf.description:
Change from the first to the latest present estimate in `points`.
Absent when fewer than two sessions produced an estimate.

LiftView.description: A number of sets at one weight and rep count.

amrap.description: When true, `reps` is a floor rather than a target — 5/3/1's "5+".

plates_per_side.description:
Plates for **one** side of the bar, largest first, empty for anything
that is not a barbell.

Computed server-side and sent, never derived by the client (D-11). The
athlete is standing at the rack holding a phone, and "112.5 kg" is a
worse answer than "bar + 25, 20, 1.25 per side".

weight.description:
Kilograms, already rounded **down** to something that can actually be
loaded (D-04).

LoggedSetView.description: One set as it was recorded.

oneOf.description:
Why this set drifted, if the athlete said. Null for every set logged
before the chips existed, and for every deviation they walked past.

label.description:
Resolved from the compiled registry, for the same reason the session
payload carries it: a browser cannot look a key up in a Rust `static`.
Cues are not repeated here — a history row is read, not performed.

logged_at.description:
When this set was logged or skipped, as the phone recorded it (D-10).
Null for anything logged before timing existed.

note.description:
What the athlete wrote about this set. Null for every set logged
before notes existed, and for every set they had nothing to say about.

refresh_token.description:
The refresh token to kill, ending the session on this device. Optional
so a client that only holds an access token can still revoke it.

LongestInterval.description: The longest single gap in the session.

position.description:
The set the interval ended at — the one that was logged late, not the
one before it.

MaxesDocument.description:
One athlete's maxes, keyed by exercise.

The same shape in both directions, so the client's form state and the
response are one type. Weights are bare numbers with kilogram semantics: no
unit is written into any domain type, which is what makes offering pounds
later a UI change and not a migration (D-04).

NextSession.description: The session the enrolment is currently pointing at.

blocks.description: The prescription as the athlete reads it: one entry per exercise.

focus.description:
The exercise key this session is built around, when there is one. A key
rather than a title, so it is data a client can act on.

pace.description:
When this session will be over, at the athlete's own pace (D-10).

Added in phase 5, and served here rather than on an endpoint of its own
because this is the only screen that asks the question. The peek page
shows the projection and the logger caches it with the committed session,
so a separate endpoint would be a second request that every caller of the
first one makes — and the header would then be drawable only after both
landed. It also keeps the *offline* story intact: what the phone caches at
commit is one response, and the pace is in it.

The cost is one more query on a read-only handler, over the same
enrolments the athlete already owns. Peeking still writes nothing (D-08).

prescribed_sets.description:
The same prescription as the athlete *logs* it: every set, expanded and
numbered.

Committing to a session materialises every prescribed set locally with
`status: pending` (D-08), and this is that list, already built. It is
here rather than left to the client because `position` is a persisted
key — `workout_sets` is unique on `(workout_id, position)` — and a number
that the server enforces should be a number the server issued. It also
keeps the round trip symmetric: what comes back in `POST /v1/workouts` is
this list with the `actual_*` fields and a status filled in.

PaceProjection.description:
What the session header needs, with the arithmetic already done.

Every field is a fact about *this* athlete and *this* session. There is
deliberately nothing here that would let a client recompute the median for
itself, because a client that could would eventually be asked to.

can_project.description:
Whether the athlete has logged enough to project from (D-10).

Not the same question as `projected_seconds != null`, though today they
answer together: this one is about the athlete's history, and a session
with nothing prescribed in it would have a pace to project *from* and
nothing to project *onto*. A client branching on "do I show the finish
time" wants this one, and a name reads better at the call site than a
null check whose meaning has to be looked up.

median_seconds_per_set.description:
The athlete's median seconds per set, or `null` when there is not enough
history to say.

Carried so the logger can re-project as sets are logged, with no network
(D-09). It is a measurement the server made, not an input the client is
expected to reason about.

projected_seconds.description:
How long this whole session should take at that pace, in seconds.

Whole seconds, and every prescribed set counted — this is the number the
peek screen shows before a single set exists to be remaining. `null`
whenever there is no pace, because an invented finish time is worse than
none, for the same reason an invented progress denominator is (D-03).

sample_size.description:
How many of the recent sessions were usable — the number the floor is
compared against, not the number of sessions looked at.

Sent because "not yet" is a more useful answer with a count attached: a
client can say "one more session" rather than going quiet for reasons the
athlete cannot see.

PlateChangeView.description:
What comes off the bar and what goes on, to get to this set's weight
(D-04).

Mirrored from [`athletos_training::PlateChange`] because the training crate
depends on `serde`, `serde_json` and `thiserror` and nothing else (D-15),
so it cannot carry a `ToSchema` of its own.

add.description: Per side, largest first — the order they go on.

plates_per_side.description:
What this leaves on the bar, largest first. Sums to
`prescribed_weight`, and is deliberately not always the greedy
breakdown that `plates_per_side` carries.

remove.description: Per side, outermost first — the order they actually come off.

PrescribedSet.description: One prescribed set, ready to be logged.

label.description: The exercise's display name, resolved from the compiled registry.

oneOf.description:
The change from the bar as the previous set of this exercise left it
(D-04).

`None` for anything not loaded with plates. Additive (D-12):
`plates_per_side` above is untouched and stays the canonical greedy
breakdown, so `LiftView` and any client already reading it are
unaffected.

Chained within an exercise and **reset to an empty bar between them** —
across exercises the previous stack is not on the bar being walked to,
and possibly not even the same bar.

plates_per_side.description:
The same breakdown [`LiftView::plates_per_side`] carries, repeated here.

Added in phase 4. The logger walks `prescribed_sets`, not `blocks`, and
the athlete needs the plates on the screen they are actually looking at.
Without this the client has to join the two lists — by position, which
means reimplementing this module's expansion order, or by
`(exercise, weight)`, which is a lookup the server can simply answer. A
few duplicated floats are cheaper than either (D-11).

position.description: Order within the session, from zero. Persisted, and unique per workout.

ProblemDetails.description:
RFC 9457 problem details. `type` is omitted until we publish stable problem
type URIs; consumers should branch on `status` plus `title` for now.

detail.description: Human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence.

status.description: HTTP status code, repeated in the body per RFC 9457.

title.description: Short, human-readable summary of the problem type.

ProgramCatalogue.description:
The catalogue, in registry order.

An object rather than a bare array so that the day this needs a cursor, a
count or a per-athlete fit marker, it can have one without changing the type
of the response (D-12).

ProgramLength.description:
Whether the program ends.

The same distinction the session payload's `progress.total` makes at runtime:
a fixed block has an honest denominator, an open-ended one has none and must
not be given an invented one (D-03).

ProgramRecoveryDemand.description:
How much the program costs to recover from — the axis D-01 cares about most.
Three coarse steps on purpose: it is a warning, not a measurement.

ProgramSummary.description:
Everything an athlete needs in order to judge whether a program fits.

There is no fit score and no ranking (D-01). `recovery_demand` and
`estimated_session_minutes` lead because they are the two axes that matter
to someone who over-reaches and who has an hour — a 75-minute program should
announce itself before enrolment, not in week three.

estimated_session_minutes.description: Wall-clock minutes for a typical session, including rest.

key.description: Stable key. This is what `POST /v1/enrollments` takes.

required_maxes.description:
The one-rep maxes this program refuses to start without (D-04).

Here so that a client can render the maxes form *before* enrolling,
without holding its own copy of which lifts which program wants. The
alternative was the 422 from `POST /v1/enrollments`, which names one
missing key at a time and only after the athlete has pressed the button.

Labels are resolved from the compiled exercise registry for the same
reason `BlockView` resolves them: a browser cannot look a key up in a
Rust `static`, and a `/v1/exercises` endpoint to cache would be a round
trip before the first form renders.

weighted_exercises.description:
Every loaded exercise this program may prescribe and therefore allows
an enrolment-specific percentage adjustment for.

ProgressView.description: Sessions completed, and the denominator if there is an honest one.

total.description:
`null` for an open-ended program. A client showing a percentage needs
this; one that invented a denominator would be lying (D-03).

ReadoutView.description:
One number a program is currently working from, and what kind of number it
is.

The mirror of the engine's `Readout`, with the exercise's display name added
the way `BlockView` adds it — a browser cannot look a key up in a Rust
`static`, and this list is short enough that a second round trip to label it
would be absurd.

There is no PUT for any of this and there must not be. A training max is the
governor a program applies to an athlete who over-reaches (D-01), and letting
them nudge it after a session that felt easy is letting them undo the
restraint (D-04). Visible and read-only is the whole shape of the decision:
the athlete may watch the number, and may not touch it.

exercise.description: The exercise this number applies to, as a registry key.

exercise_label.description: The exercise's display name, resolved from the compiled registry.

label.description:
What the number *is*, in the program's own words.

This is the field that stops the screen lying. "126" next to an entered
max of 140 is inexplicable; "Training max 126" against "Entered 1RM 140"
is the program doing its job. Only the program knows which it is — 5/3/1
took 90% and has been moving it ever since, a fixed block took the number
straight and froze it — so the words come from there and not from here.

weight.description:
Kilograms, unrounded. Unlike a prescribed weight this is not something to
load on a bar; it is the number the loadable weights are derived from
(D-04).

RecordedOutcome.description:
How a session that is already recorded turned out.

A second enum rather than a `Serialize` on [`WorkoutOutcome`], because the
two vocabularies are genuinely different sizes: a client may only ever
*claim* `completed` or `cut_short`, but it must be able to *read* the
`auto_closed` the stale-session sweep writes (D-08). Collapsing them into one
type would mean either letting a client claim `auto_closed` or hiding it from
the history, and both are worse than two enums that happen to overlap.

refresh_token.description: The opaque refresh token most recently issued to this client.

display_name.description:
The athlete's own name, shown back to them and used as context the
password may not be built out of.

password.description:
Checked against the guessability policy of NIST SP 800-63B-4 §3.1.1.2
before the account exists — see `auth::password`.

ReplaceExerciseAdjustments.description: The complete adjustment document supplied by a client.

adjustments.description: Integer percentages keyed by exercise. Zero removes an adjustment.

RequiredMax.description: One lift a program needs a max for, ready to be a labelled form field.

SessionFigures.description: One session, for the load panel and the drift band.

load_planned_kg.description:
Summed over **every** set the session prescribed, whatever its status —
unlike [`crate::report::SessionReport::load_prescribed_kg`], which sums
only the done sets on the finish-screen receipt. That field answers
"how far did the weight I actually lifted drift from what was asked?",
uncontaminated by work not done. This one answers a different question:
"how much did the program ask for, whether or not I did it?" — so a
session with half its sets skipped reads as a shortfall here rather
than as perfect compliance. Both are correct for their own panel, which
is exactly why they carry different names on `/v1` rather than one
field meaning two things depending which endpoint sent it.

SessionReport.description: What the finish screen says, computed here so no client has to (D-11).

average_duration_seconds.description:
The athlete's average across this **enrolment's** other recorded
sessions — same block, same training max, so it compares like with
like. `None` below three of them, the same rule and the same reason as
[`crate::pace`]: not shown before there is data to compute it from.

oneOf.description: `None` when no two sets carry believable stamps.

load_moved_kg.description: Summed over **done sets only**, as performed.

load_prescribed_kg.description:
Summed over the same done sets, as asked for. The gap between the two
is weight drift, uncontaminated by work not done.

sets_over.description:
Done sets lifted heavier than prescribed. The count is the part that
can be acted on: a kilogram total alone does not distinguish one wild
set from twelve small ones.

weight_changes.description:
Done sets whose actual weight differed from what was prescribed,
grouped in the order each exact change was first performed.

discarded_intervals.description:
Intervals thrown away as impossible — negative, or over the ceiling.

Reported rather than hidden. When this is not zero the totals below add
up to less than the wall clock, and the screen has to be able to say why
instead of leaving the athlete to notice the arithmetic does not work.

exercises.description:
Per exercise, in the order the exercises were first performed.

Order matters and is not alphabetical: an athlete reading this is
walking back through their own session, and the main lift they opened
with belongs at the top.

lead_in_seconds.description:
Commit to the first set logged: walking in, changing, warming up.

`None` when no set carries a stamp, which is also when the whole
structure is absent — see [`compute`].

oneOf.description:
The single longest interval, and which set closed it.

Worth surfacing on its own because it is usually the answer. An hour
that ran to eighty minutes is rarely uniformly slower; it is one gap
where something else happened.

tail_seconds.description:
The last set logged to the end of the session. `None` while the session
is still open, since there is nothing to measure to.

unstamped_sets.description:
How many sets carried no stamp at all.

Not the same as `discarded_intervals`: this is work that was never
measured, that one is a measurement that could not be believed.

exercises.description: Display metadata for this revision, also available before sign-in.

SubmittedSet.description:
One set: what was asked for and what happened (D-07).

Four numbers, not two. Going heavier than prescribed means editing the
number, and it is logged as edited — a cap would produce either dishonest
logs or an abandoned app, and honesty must never cost more than dishonesty.

actual_weight.description:
Required when `status` is `done`; the schema will not record a set as
done with no numbers, because that is a hole in every drift query that
will ever run over this table.

oneOf.description:
Why this set was lifted at something other than its prescription (D-07).

Optional and additively so (D-12). **Only a `done` set may carry one**,
and only when its weight actually differs — see `validate`. That is not
tidiness: a reason on a set that was never reached arrives with a null
`actual_weight`, the check constraint refuses it, and the whole
submission goes down over a chip tapped forty minutes earlier.

logged_at.description:
When the athlete tapped Log or Skip for this set, from the phone's clock
at that moment (D-10).

Optional, and additively so (D-12): a client that does not send it still
submits a valid workout, it simply has no timing to show afterwards.
Stamped on the device rather than here because the logger runs offline
and a submission can arrive hours late — a server clock would be
measuring when the queue flushed, not when the work happened.

Not validated against `started_at` and `ended_at`. A stamp outside them
is a phone whose clock moved, which is a fact about the measurement
rather than a malformed request, and refusing the submission would cost
the athlete a whole session's log over it. `timing` discards the
intervals it cannot believe instead.

note.description:
What the athlete wrote about this set, if anything (D-07).

Optional and additively so (D-12). Blank and whitespace-only strings
normalise to `None` rather than being refused — a note that was typed
and then cleared is not an error, and the athlete is holding a phone
with chalk on their hands.

Over 500 characters is a 422 naming the position. Truncating would
store something other than what was written, which is worse than
refusing it.

position.description:
From `prescribed_sets[].position` in the session payload. Unique within
the submission.

TokenPair.description:
A new pair of credentials. The refresh token is single-use: the next call to
`/v1/auth/refresh` invalidates it and returns its successor.

refresh_token.description: Opaque refresh token — not a JWT, and revocable.

refresh_token_expires_at.description: When the refresh token stops working, RFC 3339.

TrendPoint.description: One session's contribution to a lift's trend.

drift_kg.description:
Signed: positive is heavier than prescribed, negative lighter. Summed
over that session's done sets of this lift, against the same sets'
prescriptions, so it is weight drift uncontaminated by work not done.

estimate.description:
The best (highest) estimate across that session's done sets of this
lift. A point with no done sets is never emitted, so this is `None`
only when every done set failed to produce an estimate — each one
carrying no weight or no reps, [`athletos_training::estimate`]'s own
two absence cases. One weightless set among several does not null this
field; the max is taken across sets, so a single done set with a real
weight and rep count is enough. A set above the rep ceiling still
contributes an estimate: the ceiling caps what the formula reads
rather than refusing the set (D-13, amended).

load_moved_kg.description: Kilograms moved by done sets of this exercise in this workout.

reasons.description:
Every reason the athlete gave on this lift that session. Travels on
every point; the screen renders them only on downward moves, and that
test is presentation rather than a fact about training.

training_max.description:
What the program was prescribing from during that session. `None` for
every session logged before `enrollment_advances` existed — the chart
must draw a gap rather than a zero.

training_max_label.description:
What kind of number `training_max` is — `Readout::TRAINING_MAX` when
the program derived it and moves it on its own, `Readout::ENTERED_MAX`
when a prescriptive program has none to report and the athlete's own
typed number stands in so the chart draws a line rather than a gap.
Present exactly when `training_max` is, and absent in exactly the same
cases — never one without the other.

Not decoration: without this field the two numbers are indistinguishable
on the wire, which is precisely the confusion D-04 introduced the label
to prevent — "so the two can sit on one screen without either being
mistaken for the other." A client that dropped this field would render
an entered 1RM under the name reserved for a governor that climbs on its
own.

Unit.description:
What a figure is measured in. A tag, not a display string — the client
decides whether 3600 seconds reads as "1:00" or "60 min" (D-04).

WeightChange.description: One exact weight change, grouped across matching done sets.

WeightedExercise.description:
One adjustable exercise, labelled for a client that cannot read Rust's
compiled registry.

WorkoutDetail.description:
One workout, expanded.

The summary is nested rather than flattened so that the two responses cannot
drift: a field added to the history row is a field this endpoint gains for
free, and there is exactly one place that builds it.

sets.description:
Every set as it was logged, in position order — including the ones never
done. Both the prescribed and the actual numbers, because drift is the
thing this screen exists to show (D-07, D-13).

oneOf.description:
Where the hour went, when the sets carry stamps to work it out from.

Absent rather than empty for a session logged before timing existed, so
a client cannot render a breakdown of nothing (D-10).

WorkoutHistory.description: A page of history, newest first.

limit.description: The limit actually applied, which is not always the one asked for.

total.description:
Every workout matching the filter, not just this page — what a "load
more" control needs in order to know when to stop.

WorkoutOutcome.description:
How the session ended, as the athlete may report it.

Deliberately missing the schema's third value, `auto_closed`. That one
belongs to the sweep that closes a session left open past three hours (D-08),
and a client must not be able to claim it.

WorkoutReceipt.description: What the server recorded, and where the program stands afterwards.

duplicate.description:
True when this submit was a retry of one already accepted, and therefore
changed nothing. The status code says the same thing: 201 the first time,
200 for every retry.

progress.description:
Progress *after* the submit. A retry reports the same numbers the first
attempt did, which is the whole point.

summary.description:
What this session cost, and how it compares (D-08, amended).

Present on a retry too, and computed the same way — see `recorded_report`.

week.description:
Where in the program this session sat — decided by the server from the
enrolment's state, not taken from the request (D-11).

WorkoutSubmission.description: A finished session, as the phone recorded it.

oneOf.description:
Required when `outcome` is `cut_short`, and refused otherwise. The one
question asked when a session ends early; the program advances whatever
the answer is (D-08).

enrollment_id.description: Must belong to the authenticated athlete. Someone else's is a 404.

id.description:
**Minted by the client**, before the session started and before it had a
network, and the idempotency key for this whole endpoint (D-09).

A UUIDv7 by convention, because time-ordered ids cluster in the primary
key's btree. It is not *checked* to be v7: the idempotency comes from the
primary key and works for any uuid, whereas refusing a v4 would strand a
queued offline workout in a retry loop it could never get out of, with no
action the athlete could take to fix it.

sets.description:
Every set of the session, including the ones that were never done.

`pending` and `skipped` are first-class outcomes rather than absent rows:
what was prescribed and not performed is precisely how "work not done"
becomes the second axis of drift (D-07, D-08).

started_at.description:
Wall clock from the phone, stamped when the athlete committed to the
session — never when they merely looked at it (D-08).

WorkoutSummary.description:
One row of the history list.

Exactly what a history row shows and nothing else: when, which program,
where in it, how long it took, and how it ended. `notes` and the set list are
on the detail endpoint, because they are what the row expands *into*.

duration_seconds.description:
Wall clock, in seconds — the only measure of "the hour" there is (D-10).

Subtracted here rather than left to the client. Two clients doing date
arithmetic on two timestamps is two implementations of one rule, and the
second one is written in a different language (D-11). `null` while a
session is still open, which today means never: `POST /v1/workouts`
requires both ends.

bearer_token.description: Ed25519 (EdDSA) access token from /v1/auth/login, verifiable against /.well-known/jwks.json

post.description:
__send-coins__ executes a request to send coins to a particular address.

### LND:
If neither __target_conf__, or __sat_per_vbyte__ are set, then the internal wallet will consult its fee model to determine a fee for the default confirmation target.

> 👉 See [https://api.lightning.community/?shell#sendcoins](https://api.lightning.community/?shell#sendcoins)

### c-lightning:
* Set __target_conf__ ==1: interpreted as urgent (aim for next block)
* Set __target_conf__ >=2: interpreted as normal (next 4 blocks or so, **default**)
* Set __target_cont__ >=10: interpreted as slow (next 100 blocks or so)
* If __sat_per_vbyte__ is set then __target_conf__ is ignored and vbytes (sipabytes) will be used.

> 👉 See [https://lightning.readthedocs.io/lightning-txprepare.7.html](https://lightning.readthedocs.io/lightning-txprepare.7.html)

### Sending all onchain funds
> ℹ️ Keep the following points in mind when sending all onchain funds:

* The response object currently will state __"amount": 0__ even if __send_all__ is set to __true__ and the transaction was successfully submitted to the mempool. [GitHub issue](https://github.com/fusion44/blitz_api/issues/196)
* If __send_all__ is set to __true__, the __amount__ field must be set to __0__.
* If the __amount__ field is greater than __0__, the __send_all__ field must be __false__.
  * The API will return an error if neither or both conditions are met at the same time.
* If __send_all__ is set to __true__ the amount of satoshis to send will be calculated by subtracting the fee from the wallet balance.
* If the wallet balance is not sufficient to cover the fee, the call will fail.
* The call will __not__ close any channels.
* The implementation may keep a reserve of funds if there are still open channels.

200.description: Either an error or a SendCoinsResponse object on success

412.description: When not enough funds are available.

Transaction amount in satoshis

* value in millisatoshis of the invoice if *unsettled*

* amount sent in millisatoshis

time_stamp.title: Time Stamp
time_stamp.description:
The unix timestamp in seconds for the transaction.

The timestamp can mean different things in different situations:

#### Lightning Invoice
* Creation date for in-flight or failed invoices
* Settle date for succeeded invoices

#### On-chain
* Creation date for transaction waiting in the mempool
* Timestamp of the block where this transaction is included

#### Lightning Payment

status.description:
The status of the transaction. Depending on the transaction category this can be different values:

May have different meanings in different situations:
#### unknown
An unknown state was found.

#### in_flight
* A lightning payment is being sent
* An invoice is waiting for the incoming payment
* An on-chain transaction is waiting in the mempool

#### succeeded
* A lighting payment was successfully sent
* An incoming payment was received for an invoice
* An on-chain transaction was included in a block

#### failed
* A lightning payment attempt which could not be completed (no route found, insufficient funds, ...)
* An invoice is expired or some other error happened

add_index.description: The index of this invoice. Each newly created invoice will increment this index making it monotonically increasing. CLN and LND handle ids differently. LND will generate an auto incremented integer id, while CLN will use a user supplied string id. To unify both, we auto generate an id for CLN and use the add_index for LND.For `LND` this will be an `integer` in string form. This is auto generated by LND. For `CLN` this will be a `string`. If the invoice was generated by BlitzAPI, this will be a [Firebase-like PushID](https://firebase.blog/posts/2015/02/the-2120-ways-to-ensure-unique_68). info.title: HUSST Tickethub API
info.description:
This API provides secure management of tickets associated with transit tokens. It supports:
 - Storing and updating tickets.
 - Retrieving ticket information for inspection and validation processes.
 - Managing the full ticket lifecycle, including actions such as blocking, terminating (e.g., for non-payment), deleting, or reassigning a ticket to a different transit token.

Security model:
  - Create, update, and delete operations (POST, PATCH, DELETE) require OAuth2 JWT Bearer Tokens combined with mutual TLS (mTLS).
  - View and Validation operations (GET) require OAuth2 JWT Bearer Tokens (certificate-bound). Client mTLS is not required for read operations.

  Based on the provided certificates, it is determined which data (e.g., for which CCP) can be accessed and written.

post.summary: Create new ticket for a transit token

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: Unique key to ensure idempotent ticket creation requests.

403.description: Forbidden

409.description: Conflict - Ticket already exists and idempotency key doesn't match

500.description: Internal Server Error

get.summary: Retrieve all tickets to a transit token
get.description: Retrieve all tickets to a transit token. For inspection purposes, the `inspection` flag must be set to true and only tickets that are still valid (time-based) or recently expired are returned. Tickets are returned if the current time is within the validity range plus an operator-defined tolerance window. Tickets whose tokenType matches the specified value and whose transitToken matches according to the rules of that tokenType are returned.

bearerAuth.description:
OAuth2 Bearer Token (JWT) with certificate binding per RFC 8705.
Client certificate binding is required for write operations. Read operations validate the certificate binding claim but do not require client mTLS.

Required claims:
- `cnf.x5t#S256`: SHA-256 thumbprint of the client certificate (base64url-encoded)
- `vdv_role`: VDV-KA role (`so`, `ccp`)
- `vdv_org_id`: VDV-KA Organization ID (integer)
- `scope`: Authorized scopes (see below)

Available scopes:
- `view:token`: View ticket information from transit token (SO, CCP)
- `validate:token`: Validate ticket from transit token (SO, CCP)
- `replace:token`: Replace transit token by a new transit token (CCP)
- `create:ticket`: Create tickets for transit token (CCP)
- `update:ticket`: Update tickets for transit token (CCP)
- `delete:ticket`: Delete tickets from transit token (CCP)

Role permissions:
- SO (Dienstleister): `view:token`, `validate:token` - Can read all tickets for inspection
- CCP (Kundenvertragspartner): `view:token`, `validate:token`, `create:ticket`, `update:ticket`, `delete:ticket`, `replace:token` - Can manage own tickets

mtls.description:
Mutual TLS with X.509 client certificate following VDV-KA PKI structure.

Certificate Subject DN format:
- CN: `{role}{vdv_org_id_decimal}.{domain}` (e.g., `dl44.rheinbahn.de`, `kvp35000.example.de`)
- O: vdv_org_id in hexadecimal (e.g., `002C` for org_id 44)
- C: Country code (ISO 3166-1 alpha-2, e.g., `DE`)

Role prefixes (variable length, 2-3 characters):
- `dl`: Dienstleister (Service Provider / Transport Operator)
- `kvp`: Kundenvertragspartner (Customer Contract Partner / CCP)
- `pv`: Produktverantwortlicher (Product Owner)

The OrgId extracted from the certificate must match the `ccpOrgId` in write operations.

OAuth2.description:
## Authentication

Tokens should be made using the OAuth Bearer Token specification,
using the Authorization header in the request.

Here is an example:

```
GET /utilities HTTP/1.1
Host: api.stash.energy
Authorization: Bearer {token}
```

### Authentication flow

1. Get an `id` and `key` from your Stash Energy representative (one time only)
2. Send a POST command to [this URL](https://auth.api.stash.energy/60658de9-a14c-4bb9-8dc5-26d1bd003872/oauth2/v2.0/token?p=b2c_1_auth&grant_type=password&scope=openid%20032d91df-6ddf-43d3-bcc9-8015d1f5a539&client_id=032d91df-6ddf-43d3-bcc9-8015d1f5a539&response_type=token) with the following parameters in the `x-www-form-urlencoded` format:
    * username = `<id>`
    * password = `<key>`
3. Retrieve the access token from the `access_token` property of the JSON response
4. Use this token to authenticate your API requests. (Include it in the Authorization header)

**NOTE: The access token will be valid for 4 hours**

## Security best practices

* ALWAYS keep your password and access tokens in a secure location.
* DO NOT share your password or access tokens.
* NEVER check your password or access tokens into version control (ex. git).
* It is RECOMMENDED to change your password at least every 6 months.

We reserve the right to revoke access to any user who abuses the API.
